# P-016 — Replace, do not repair, platform nodes

## Statement

Bare-metal servers, hypervisor hosts, virtual machines and cluster nodes are rebuilt from a versioned image and declarative configuration; they are never patched or reconfigured in place.

## Why

In-place changes accumulate as undocumented drift that makes the next incident and the next upgrade unpredictable. Rebuilding from a known image turns every node into a reproducible artefact.

## Implications

- Every layer has an image pipeline (see the golden image pattern) and a way to drain and replace a node without service loss.
- Emergency fixes are made in the image or the configuration source, then rolled out; a manual fix is a defect to be reverted.
- Nodes are treated as disposable: no unique data lives on a node's local disk without replication or backup.

## How to verify

Pick any running node and compare its image identifier and configuration digest with the versions declared in the source repository; any node without a declared origin, or modified since its build, is a defect.

# P-017 — Workloads target a platform contract, not an implementation

## Statement

Application teams consume documented platform interfaces (compute classes, storage classes, network policies, platform APIs), never a specific hypervisor, cluster or host.

## Why

When workloads depend on implementation details, every platform upgrade or replacement becomes a migration project for every tenant.

## Implications

- The platform publishes its contract (classes, quotas, supported versions) and versions it.
- Implementation-specific features are exposed only through the contract, or not at all.
- Moving a workload between clusters or sites requires no change to its manifests beyond environment values.

## How to verify

Redeploy a reference workload on a second cluster or site of the platform using only its manifests and environment values; any required change outside those values reveals a contract leak.

# P-018 — Headroom for the loss of a failure domain

## Statement

Each platform layer keeps enough spare capacity to absorb the loss of its largest failure domain (host, rack, availability zone or site) without refusing committed workloads.

## Why

Capacity planned on average load turns a single hardware failure into a capacity incident, precisely when the platform is already degraded.

## Implications

- Capacity reports show, per layer, the load after the loss of the largest failure domain.
- Admission of new workloads stops before the headroom is consumed, not after.
- Maintenance (host evacuation, node drain) is planned against the same headroom.

## How to verify

Simulate the loss of the largest failure domain (drain or power off in a test window) and check that every committed workload is rescheduled and meets its service level.

# P-019 — Tenant isolation is enforced by the lowest shared layer

## Statement

Isolation between tenants and security zones is enforced by the lowest layer they share (network segmentation, hypervisor, dedicated clusters or node pools), not delegated to the tenants' own configuration.

## Why

An isolation that depends on each tenant configuring its workloads correctly fails the first time one of them does not.

## Implications

- Security zones map to distinct clusters, node pools or hypervisor clusters with their own network segments.
- Default-deny network policies and admission controls are owned by the platform team.
- Shared control planes are counted as part of every tenant's attack surface.

## How to verify

For each pair of security zones, show the layer that enforces the separation and run a connectivity and privilege test from one zone to the other; any path that relies on tenant configuration is a finding.

# P-020 — Every layer stays inside its supported version window

## Statement

Firmware, hypervisors, operating systems, cluster versions and platform services each have a declared supported-version window and an upgrade cadence that keeps them inside it.

## Why

Layers that fall out of support accumulate vulnerabilities and block the upgrades of the layers above them, until a forced big-bang migration.

## Implications

- The platform keeps an inventory of versions per layer with their end-of-support dates.
- Upgrades are routine, rehearsed operations planned in the run model, not projects.
- Version skew rules between adjacent layers are documented and enforced.

## How to verify

Compare the version inventory with the supported windows: any component outside its window, or with no planned upgrade before its end-of-support date, is a defect.

# PAT-012 — Image-based bare-metal provisioning pipeline

## Problem

Physical servers configured by hand or by in-place scripts drift apart, take long to rebuild and cannot be trusted after an incident.

## Forces

- Servers must be rebuilt quickly and identically, including firmware and BIOS settings.
- The provisioning chain must work when the production network is degraded.
- Hardware of several generations coexists.

## Solution

Servers are discovered and driven through their baseboard management controller over a dedicated out-of-band network (Redfish or IPMI). A provisioning service boots them from the network or virtual media, applies firmware and BIOS profiles declared in version control, and writes a signed operating system image; host-specific values come from an inventory source of truth. Decommissioning wipes and releases the server through the same chain.

## Trade-offs

- Requires a reliable inventory and an out-of-band network with its own access controls.
- Firmware profiles per hardware generation must be maintained.
- Initial investment is higher than scripted installs.

## When not to use this

Very small fleets (a handful of servers) with no rebuild target, where the chain would cost more than it saves.

# PAT-013 — Golden image factory

## Problem

Base images for servers, virtual machines and containers are built ad hoc, with unknown content and unknown vulnerabilities.

## Forces

- Images must be reproducible and traceable to their sources.
- Vulnerabilities must be fixed by rebuilding, not by patching running nodes.
- Consumers need a small, stable set of supported bases.

## Solution

A pipeline builds every base image from versioned definitions, scans it for vulnerabilities and configuration drift against the security baseline, produces a software bill of materials, signs it and publishes it to a registry. Consumers may only use signed images from that registry; admission controls reject others. Images are rebuilt on a schedule and whenever a critical vulnerability is published.

## Trade-offs

- The catalogue of supported images must stay small, or maintenance explodes.
- Rebuild cadence must be matched by the ability to roll out new images.

## When not to use this

Environments without automated rollout: a factory that produces images nobody deploys only adds cost.

# PAT-014 — Rolling host maintenance on hypervisor clusters

## Problem

Hypervisor patches and hardware maintenance require downtime of the virtual machines they host.

## Forces

- Virtual machines must stay available during host maintenance.
- Maintenance must be routine, not an exceptional operation.
- Some workloads cannot be live-migrated.

## Solution

Hosts are updated one at a time: each host enters maintenance mode, its virtual machines are live-migrated to the other hosts (within the headroom kept for one failure domain), the host is updated or rebuilt, validated and returned to the cluster. Workloads that cannot migrate are identified in advance and scheduled with their owners. Anti-affinity rules keep replicas of a service on different hosts.

## Trade-offs

- Requires spare capacity equal to at least one host per cluster.
- Shared storage or storage replication is needed for live migration.

## When not to use this

Single-host deployments, or workloads tied to host hardware (pass-through devices) without a failover design.

# PAT-015 — Cluster fleet reconciled from version control

## Problem

Container clusters configured by hand diverge from each other and from their documentation; recreating one after a failure is slow and uncertain.

## Forces

- Several clusters per environment and security zone must stay consistent.
- Cluster configuration changes must be reviewed.
- A cluster must be recreatable from scratch.

## Solution

Each cluster is declared in a repository (version, node pools, add-ons, policies) and a reconciliation agent continuously applies that declaration, reporting drift. Common add-ons are defined once and specialised by environment overlays. Creating a cluster means adding its declaration; recreating it means re-applying it on new infrastructure.

## Trade-offs

- The repository and the reconciliation agents become critical components and need their own resilience.
- Secrets need a dedicated mechanism rather than plain files in the repository.

## When not to use this

One-off experimental clusters with a lifetime of days, where declarative management is overhead.

# PAT-016 — Node pools segregated by workload class

## Problem

Heterogeneous workloads sharing the same nodes interfere with each other: noisy neighbours, special hardware wasted, security zones mixed.

## Forces

- Some workloads need special hardware or dedicated capacity.
- Platform components must keep running when tenant workloads misbehave.
- Capacity must be planned per class.

## Solution

Nodes are grouped into pools by workload class (platform system components, general workloads, stateful, accelerated hardware, and one pool per security zone when zones share a cluster). Taints and labels restrict scheduling to the intended pool, resource quotas and priorities protect platform components, and capacity is planned per pool.

## Trade-offs

- More pools means more fragmentation and a larger total headroom.
- Scheduling rules must be maintained with the workload catalogue.

## When not to use this

Small clusters with homogeneous workloads, where pools fragment capacity for no benefit.

# PAT-017 — Controlled ingress and egress gateways

## Problem

Workloads that each open their own exposure and reach any external destination make north-south traffic impossible to control and audit.

## Forces

- Exposure of services must follow the security zoning.
- Outbound traffic must be restricted to declared destinations.
- Application teams need self-service without bypassing controls.

## Solution

All inbound traffic enters through platform-owned ingress gateways that terminate TLS, apply authentication and rate limits, and route by declared routes. All outbound traffic leaves through egress gateways with an allow-list of destinations per tenant, logged centrally. Default-deny network policies block direct paths. Tenants declare routes and egress needs through the platform API.

## Trade-offs

- Gateways are shared components that must be scaled and made highly available.
- Allow-lists need an owner and a review process.

## When not to use this

Isolated batch environments with no inbound exposure and no outbound connectivity.

# PAT-018 — Stateful workloads with backups outside their cluster

## Problem

Databases and other stateful services on container platforms are lost with their cluster or storage system, because their protection lives in the same failure domain.

## Forces

- Stateful services must survive the loss of a whole cluster.
- Restores must be tested, not assumed.
- Application teams should not build their own backup systems.

## Solution

Stateful services are run by operators that manage replication and consistent snapshots, and a platform backup service copies data and the corresponding manifests to storage located in another failure domain (another site or an independent object store). Restoration into a fresh cluster is automated and exercised on a schedule, with measured recovery times.

## Trade-offs

- Backup storage and restore tests have a recurring cost.
- Operators add their own lifecycle to manage.

## When not to use this

Ephemeral data that can be recomputed from an upstream source faster than it could be restored.

# PAT-019 — Golden paths through a declarative platform API

## Problem

Application teams obtain platform resources through tickets or ad hoc scripts, which is slow and produces inconsistent, unsupported configurations.

## Forces

- Teams need self-service within minutes.
- The platform team must keep control of security and cost.
- Configurations must stay reproducible.

## Solution

The platform exposes a small set of golden paths (service templates, databases, queues, environments) through a declarative API: teams commit a short resource description, the platform validates it against policies and provisions compliant resources. Templates encode the security baseline and observability by default; exceptions go through review.

## Trade-offs

- Golden paths must be maintained as a product with its own roadmap.
- Teams with unusual needs still need an exception path.

## When not to use this

Organisations with a single application team, where a direct collaboration costs less than a platform product.

# ADR-0017 — Provision bare-metal servers from images rather than in-place configuration

## Context

Physical servers are provisioned with a mix of manual installs and configuration scripts; rebuild times and drift are not acceptable for the target recovery objectives.

## Options considered

### Option A — Image-based provisioning
Signed images written through the out-of-band network; host values from the inventory. Fast, reproducible rebuilds; needs an image factory.

### Option B — Configuration management in place
Install once, converge with a configuration tool. Familiar; drift and long rebuilds remain.

### Option C — Manual installation with checklists
No tooling cost; neither reproducible nor auditable.

## Decision

Option A: image-based provisioning through the out-of-band network, with firmware and BIOS profiles in version control.

## Consequences

- An image factory and an out-of-band provisioning service become platform components.
- Rebuilding a server becomes the default remediation for a compromised or drifted host.

# ADR-0018 — Run container clusters on virtual machines by default

## Context

Container clusters can run directly on physical servers or on virtual machines. Most workloads do not need direct hardware access, but some (accelerated hardware, very low latency, licensing constraints) do.

## Options considered

### Option A — Virtual machines by default, bare metal by exception
Node replacement and maintenance reuse the virtualization layer; exceptions justified per workload class.

### Option B — Bare metal only
No virtualization overhead or licence; node lifecycle and density are harder to manage.

### Option C — Virtual machines only
Uniform; excludes workloads that need direct hardware access.

## Decision

Option A: cluster nodes are virtual machines by default; bare-metal node pools are allowed for justified workload classes, each justification recorded.

## Consequences

- The virtualization layer's headroom must include the container nodes.
- Bare-metal node pools follow the image-based provisioning pipeline.

# ADR-0019 — One container cluster per environment and security zone

## Context

Tenants and environments can share clusters (separated by namespaces) or get dedicated clusters. The security zoning of the platform requires strong separation between zones.

## Options considered

### Option A — Cluster per environment and security zone
Strong isolation and independent upgrades; more clusters to operate.

### Option B — Shared clusters with namespace isolation
Fewer clusters; isolation depends on policies inside a shared control plane.

### Option C — One cluster per application
Maximum isolation; operational cost and waste become prohibitive.

## Decision

Option A: at least one cluster per environment and per security zone; namespaces separate tenants inside a zone. Fleet management is declarative to keep the number of clusters manageable.

## Consequences

- Cluster fleet reconciliation from version control is required.
- Capacity headroom is planned per cluster.

# ADR-0020 — Use a conformant container orchestration distribution within a supported version window

## Context

Several container orchestration distributions are available; the platform must stay portable and within vendor support.

## Options considered

### Option A — Conformant distribution with a supported window
Portability through conformance; upgrades at least twice a year to stay in support.

### Option B — Heavily customised build
Tailored features; upgrades and support become the platform team's burden.

### Option C — Managed service of a single provider
Less operational load; dependency on one provider and its location.

## Decision

Option A: a distribution that passes the upstream conformance tests, kept within the supported version window with a documented upgrade cadence; provider-specific extensions are exposed only through the platform contract.

## Consequences

- The run model includes recurring cluster upgrades.
- Workload manifests must avoid deprecated interfaces, checked in the delivery pipelines.

# ADR-0021 — Expose platform services through a declarative API

## Context

Application teams request databases, queues and environments through tickets; lead times are long and configurations inconsistent.

## Options considered

### Option A — Declarative platform API with golden paths
Self-service, policy-checked and reproducible; the API and its templates must be built and maintained.

### Option B — Ticket-based provisioning
No new tooling; slow and inconsistent.

### Option C — Direct access to infrastructure APIs
Fast; bypasses the security baseline and cost controls.

## Decision

Option A: platform services are requested through versioned resource descriptions submitted to a declarative platform API, validated against policies before provisioning.

## Consequences

- The platform team runs the API and its templates as a product.
- Exceptions to golden paths require a reviewed request.
